headline: Tech-led shock fades to a cautious bounce ahead of jobs data
body: Thursday brought the sharpest single-day shock to U.S. equities in over a year: the Nasdaq Composite fell roughly 5.5% and slid into correction territory, more than 10% below its early-October record, while the Nasdaq 100 dropped over 6% in its worst session since the pandemic-era volatility of March 2020. The S&P 500 and Dow each posted their worst days since April 2025, down roughly 4% and 3.5% respectively, and chipmakers bore the brunt — the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost more than 12%, with Nvidia down over 9%. Coverage points to no single trigger, instead blaming a convergence of worries: that AI infrastructure spending is outrunning AI revenue, and that shifting post-midterm political dynamics could complicate the pace of data-center buildout. Roughly $2.5 trillion in market value was erased in the session.

Friday's open shows some stabilization rather than panic: Nasdaq 100 futures were pointing modestly higher in early trading, a partial, not full, retracement of Thursday's loss. The bigger swing variable is macro — today's delayed October jobs report lands against a backdrop where rate expectations have gotten noticeably less settled; some trackers now put the odds of continued Fed tightening near two-thirds, a marked shift from the heavy easing bets priced in just weeks earlier. That repricing removes some of the cushion dip-buyers had been leaning on through the year. Retail-sentiment chatter around the selloff was thin and inconsistent in today's search results, so this read leans more on confirmed price action and wire coverage than on any clear signal from social or retail positioning.
